intro.t:
Each dot on this map stands for 250 people, placed at the polling place where they are registered. Blue dots are votes for the Bolsonaro camp, red for Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, amber for people on the roll who did not vote, and grey for everyone else.

Scroll down to see where the vote moved between the first rounds of 2022 and 2026.

overview.t:
Lula's share of the vote fell in 5,468 of Brazil's 5,570 municipalities. In 2022 he led Jair Bolsonaro in the first round, 48.4 percent to 43.2 percent. This year Flávio Bolsonaro finished first, with 47.0 percent to Lula's 45.2 percent.

The losses were spread across the country. Lula's share slipped in the North and the Southeast and fell further in the South. He still won the Northeast by a wide margin. More than 700 municipalities that voted for him four years ago backed the Bolsonaro camp this time.

Drag the divider to compare 2022, on the left, with 2026.

The ballot is secret. These maps show how places voted. They cannot show which voters changed their minds.

arrows.t:
Each arrow is a municipality. Arrows point right and are blue where the margin moved toward the Bolsonaro camp from 2022 to 2026, and left and red where it moved toward Lula. Longer arrows mean bigger shifts.

The margin moved toward the Bolsonaro camp in 5,512 of 5,570 municipalities. The next three views sort them by how much Lula lost.

held.t:
Lula's share held or rose in 102 municipalities, shown here. Most are big cities: Rio de Janeiro, Brasília, Fortaleza, Manaus, Recife, Belém, Maceió, Aracaju, Niterói and Santos. Together they cast 12 percent of the valid vote.

The totals at the top now count only these places.

slipped.t: His share fell by up to five points in 2,312 municipalities. They include São Paulo, Salvador, most mid-sized cities and much of the Northeast, and they cast 63 percent of the valid vote. Across them, Lula went from 48.0 percent to 45.6 percent.

shifted.t: In the other 3,156 municipalities his share fell by more than five points. That is more than half of Brazil's municipalities, but they cast only 26 percent of the vote. Most are small towns in the interior, the South and the Centre-West. Lula's share there dropped from 50.9 percent to 43.6 percent.

small-towns.h: The smaller the town, the bigger the shift
small-towns.t: These are the smallest quarter of municipalities, each with fewer than about 5,200 residents. 2022 is on the left of the divider. The fall in Lula's share grows steadily as places get smaller.

abstention.t:
In 2026, 33.5 million registered voters did not vote, more than voted for any candidate except the two leaders. Abstention has risen in every presidential first round since 2006, from 16.8 percent to 21.1 percent.

It rose by only 0.1 points from 2022, so it does not explain Lula's losses. He lost 3.4 million votes, and the Bolsonaro camp gained 5.0 million. In the poorest quarter of municipalities, where Lula is strongest, abstention fell 2.5 points. In the richest quarter it rose 0.9 points.

chart.title: Abstention, presidential first round (% of the roll)

northeast.t: Lula still dominates the Northeast, but his share there fell from 66.8 percent to 63.8 percent, and the Bolsonaro camp's rose 3.9 points. In Salvador he went from 67.0 percent to 65.3 percent. In Feira de Santana, Bahia's second-largest city, he fell from 61.7 percent to 57.1 percent. A few capitals held, among them Fortaleza and Recife.

capitals.t:
In the 27 state capitals, Lula's share slipped from 45.5 percent to 44.9 percent. Everywhere else it fell from 49.3 percent to 45.2 percent.

The difference is visible around Rio. The city and Niterói held. Next door, in the Baixada Fluminense and São Gonçalo, the vote moved toward the Bolsonaro camp. Lula's share in each, 2022 to 2026:

chart.title: Lula's share: capitals vs the rest

goias.t: Lula's share fell more in Goiás than in any other state, by 8.5 points. Much of the vote went to Ronaldo Caiado, a former governor of the state, who won 12.3 percent there. His votes are among the grey dots on the 2026 side.

south.h: The largest drop, in the South
south.t: The South had the largest drop of any region, 5.5 points, and Rio Grande do Sul fell 6.6. Around Caxias do Sul, in the hills of the Serra Gaúcha, Lula's share fell about five points. Abstention there also rose.

sp-classes-ac.h: In São Paulo, Lula gained in richer neighbourhoods
sp-classes-ac.t:
Within São Paulo, the pattern reverses. In neighbourhoods of classes A to C, where household heads earn on average more than four minimum wages (R$ 4,848 a month in the 2022 census), Lula's share rose from 39.6 percent to 41.9 percent. The Bolsonaro camp also gained, from 42.0 percent to 45.4 percent. Both took votes from smaller candidates. Abstention rose from 22.2 percent to 23.4 percent.

Each polling place is matched to census tracts within one kilometre. Classes are based on the income of the household head, which approximates the usual household-income definition.

sp-class-d.t: In class D neighbourhoods, where household heads earn two to four minimum wages, Lula's share fell from 47.0 percent to 45.5 percent. The Bolsonaro camp rose from 39.3 percent to 43.4 percent. Abstention went from 21.2 percent to 23.2 percent.

sp-class-e.h: …and lost the most in class E
sp-class-e.t:
The poorest neighbourhoods, class E, where household heads earn up to two minimum wages, still voted for Lula. But his share fell from 58.4 percent to 54.5 percent, and the Bolsonaro camp grew from 30.8 percent to 35.7 percent, its largest gain of the three groups. Abstention rose the most here as well, from 20.2 percent to 23.7 percent.

In São Paulo, Lula's losses came from neighbourhoods below four minimum wages, and most of all from the poorest.

religion.h: Lula fell further in Catholic towns
religion.t:
In the most Catholic quarter of municipalities, where at least 80 percent of residents are Catholic, Lula's share fell 5.3 points, from 66.5 percent to 61.2 percent. These places are mostly small and rural. The Bolsonaro camp rose from 27.7 percent to 33.5 percent, and abstention fell from 20.6 percent to 19.5 percent.

In the least Catholic quarter, mostly big cities, Lula fell 2.6 points. The most evangelical places matched the national drop of 3.3 points.

The data describes places. It does not show how Catholics voted.

chart.title: Lula's share by Catholic share of residents

who-didnt-vote.t:
About one in five registered voters did not vote. Not all of them were required to.

18–69, who must vote: 14.7 percent of the roll, and 70 percent of those who did not vote.
16–17 and 70–79, for whom voting is optional: 3.5 percent of the roll, 17 percent of non-voters.
80 and older: 2.8 percent of the roll, 13 percent of non-voters.

The 2026 age split is estimated.

over-80.t: The 2026 roll lists 297,977 voters aged 100 or older. In 2022, 99 percent of that age group did not vote. Some of the abstainers over 80 have died but remain on the roll. Without them, abstention was 18.9 percent, 0.1 points higher than in 2022.

excess-abstention.t:
Abstention is partly predictable. Some age groups and people with less schooling vote less often. For each polling place, we estimated expected abstention by applying the 2022 rates for each age and schooling group in its state to the people on its 2026 roll, then adjusted the estimates so each state's total matched its actual abstention.

The map shows, in amber, the tenth of polling places where abstention was furthest above that estimate, by 4.5 points or more. About 11 million people are registered there. Based on age and schooling, about 21 percent would be expected to stay home; 27.5 percent did. These places are spread out, led by São Paulo, Minas Gerais, Bahia and Rio Grande do Sul.

The model does not account for distance to the polling place, transport, weather or local politics. It points to places worth a closer look, and does not explain why people stayed away.

smaller-candidates.t:
In polling places that hold about a fifth of all voters, candidates other than Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro won 10 percent or more of the valid vote. Together they took 12.1 percent in these places, compared with 7.8 percent nationally. Most of these polling places are in São Paulo state and in Goiás, Ronaldo Caiado's home state, and in neighbourhoods richer than average. Flávio Bolsonaro led Lula there, 51.0 percent to 36.9 percent.

Augusto Cury, Renan Santos and Caiado won 8.7 million votes combined. A Genial/Quaest poll taken 2–3 October asked their voters how they would vote in a runoff between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro. Applying its results, about 3.9 million lean toward Flávio Bolsonaro, 1.6 million toward Lula, and 3.2 million are undecided or would back neither. That last group is larger than Flávio Bolsonaro's first-round lead of 2.2 million votes.

The poll's runoff split is national, applied here to the vote counts. It is not measured place by place.

find.t: Type the name of a municipality to see how its vote changed, compared with the country as a whole.

explore.t: Every view in this story comes from the same map. In Explore you can search for any municipality, compare the two years, show the shift arrows, split abstention by age and filter by neighbourhood or municipality. Share view creates a link to what you are looking at.

studio.filtersNote: Ranges move by number of municipalities. Totals add up the municipalities that pass; rates in small places swing widely. Every filter describes places, not voters: a municipality that is 40% Evangelical and voted Flávio doesn't show how Evangelicals voted.
